subject: Biochemistry
vignette: A 30-year-old woman is evaluated for recurrent episodes of severe abdominal pain and vomiting accompanied by dark urine, along with fragile blisters on the backs of her hands after sun exposure. Between attacks she is asymptomatic. Laboratory studies during an attack show elevated urinary ALA and porphobilinogen, and stool and urine contain large amounts of coproporphyrin III.
question: Which of the following enzyme deficiencies is most likely responsible for both the abdominal attacks and the skin lesions?
explanation_correct: Hereditary coproporphyria results from deficiency of coproporphyrinogen oxidase, which converts coproporphyrinogen III to protoporphyrinogen IX. Accumulated coproporphyrin III is excreted in urine and stool. Unlike acute intermittent porphyria, hereditary coproporphyria can cause both neurovisceral attacks and cutaneous photosensitivity.

explanation_incorrect.A: Protoporphyrinogen oxidase deficiency causes variegate porphyria, in which fecal protoporphyrin IX rather than coproporphyrin III predominates.
explanation_incorrect.B: Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase deficiency causes porphyria cutanea tarda, which produces skin fragility and uroporphyrinuria without acute attacks.
explanation_incorrect.D: Porphobilinogen deaminase deficiency causes acute intermittent porphyria, which has no cutaneous manifestations.
explanation_incorrect.E: Uroporphyrinogen III synthase deficiency causes congenital erythropoietic porphyria, a severe childhood disease with hemolytic anemia and uroporphyrin I accumulation.

educationalObjective: Hereditary coproporphyria is caused by coproporphyrinogen oxidase deficiency and is one of the porphyrias that can produce both neurovisceral attacks and photosensitive skin lesions.
